![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14243863/assets/d51a8e78f8b8c1f05e502bd98aed6a253799336765f1331d23e63ec637bcb448.png)

The diagram above shows the unit circle. Given that the $x$-coordinate of the point $P$ is $\frac{\sqrt{7}}{4},$ use the Pythagorean identity to find $\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .$
question.worked_solution:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14243863/assets/438ce908c902696b480bf9791cae089be40f9e7b2552208e13e08405496b696c.png)

Any point $(x,y)$ on the unit circle is related to the central angle $\theta $ as follows:

$$
x=\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,y=\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta 
$$

We're given that $x=\frac{\sqrt{7}}{4}$ at the point $P.$ Therefore, we have

$$
\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta =\frac{\sqrt{7}}{4}.
$$

We can use the Pythagorean identity to find $\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta :$

$$
\begin{aligned}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta +{cos}^{2}⁡\theta  & =1 \\ {sin}^{2}⁡\theta  & =1-{cos}^{2}⁡\theta  \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  & =\pm \sqrt{1-{cos}^{2}⁡\theta }\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta =\frac{\sqrt{7}}{4}$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  & =\pm \sqrt{1-{(\frac{\sqrt{7}}{4})}^{2}} \\  & =\pm \sqrt{1-\frac{7}{16}} \\  & =\pm \sqrt{\frac{9}{16}} \\  & =\pm \frac{3}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we select the positive answer since $\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta $ is positive in the first quadrant. So our final answer is $\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta =\frac{3}{4}.$
